1.pericope_label: And the angel that talked with me came again, and waked me, as a man that is wakened out of his sleep, And said unto me, What seest thou? And I said, I have looked, and behold a candlestick all of gold, with a bowl upon the top of it, and his seven lamps thereon, and seven pipes to the seven lamps, which are upon the top thereof: And two olive trees by it, one upon the right side of the bowl, and the other upon the left side thereof.

schools.summary: Ellicott treats the waking as possibly figurative, the angel having withdrawn and returned, or the whole scene a waking dream; Keil and Delitzsch weigh how far the golden candlestick answers to the sanctuary lampstand and report the pipes as fourteen, seven to each lamp.
Calvin reads the vision as the promise that the Spirit alone suffices to sustain the church without earthly helps, and defends the temple ceremony against the charge that it was a mere shadow.

Clarke gives the general sense first and then a step-by-step allegory of oil, bowl, pipes and lamps, counting seven pipes; Wesley reads the candlestick of gold as the figure of the church, its light and its purity.
Henry takes the waking at face value, the prophet overcome by weak flesh and refreshed so as to receive new discoveries.

debates.question: How many pipes did the vision show?

positions.position: Fourteen, seven to each of the two chief lamps.
Forty-nine, seven to each of the seven lamps.

debates.question: Why was the prophet asleep and woken?

positions.position: He really slept, the flesh being weak under so strange a vision, and was woken to be fresh for new discoveries.
The waking need not be literal: the angel may have withdrawn and returned, or the whole may be described after the manner of a dream.

outliers.claim: Argues that the Spirit is sufficient to preserve the church without any earthly aid, and that the ceremony of the temple was no empty shadow but a real help suited to the people's weakness.

4.pericope_label: So I answered and spake to the angel that talked with me, saying, What are these, my lord? Then the angel that talked with me answered and said unto me, Knowest thou not what these be? And I said, No, my lord. Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the Lord unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts. Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain: and he shall bring forth the headstone thereof with shoutings, crying, Grace, grace unto it. Moreover the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it; and thou shalt know that the Lord of hosts hath sent me unto you. For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the Lord, which run to and fro through the whole earth.

schools.summary: Ellicott explains why a vision is called a word, renders the levelling literally as to a plain and notes that the old Greek mistook the form for an Aramaic infinitive, and treats the question about the day of small things as equivalent to a prohibition; Keil and Delitzsch observe only that the prophet now has the general meaning with one point still obscure.
Gill offers two readings of the question put back to the prophet and identifies the great mountain either with the men obstructing the work or with the Persian monarchy and its capital.

Clarke distinguishes might as one's own strength from power as authority derived from others, and answers the world's objection about means with the flat charge that Satan lies; Wesley glosses the second term as courage and valour and finds the rule that God chooses weak instruments for mighty things.
Henry states the principle that the dawning light is not to be despised, since it will shine more and more to the perfect day.

positions.position: The men who obstructed the building, or the Persian monarchy and its capital, a mountain being the symbol of a kingdom.
The royal prohibition that had stopped the work.
A figure for the colossal difficulties raised by the neighbouring powers.

debates.question: Why is the prophet asked whether he knows what these are?

positions.position: Either to upbraid his ignorance or, preferably, to quicken his attention to the interpretation coming.

debates.question: What is the force of the question about the day of small things?

positions.position: It is equivalent to a prohibition, since no one who intended great things ever despised such a day.
It answers the taunt that these feeble Jews could do nothing, God undertaking to build by them and perfect it.
It teaches that God often chooses weak instruments, and though the beginnings be small the latter end greatly increases.

outliers.claim: Lays down that no secular arm, human prudence, earthly policy or suit at law may ever be used for founding or preserving the church, and answers the objection that such means are necessary with the three words that Satan lies.

11.pericope_label: Then answered I, and said unto him, What are these two olive trees upon the right side of the candlestick and upon the left side thereof? And I answered again, and said unto him, What be these two olive branches which through the two golden pipes empty the golden oil out of themselves? And he answered me and said, Knowest thou not what these be? And I said, No, my lord. Then said he, These are the two anointed ones, that stand by the Lord of the whole earth.

schools.summary: Ellicott corrects the rendering to bunches of olives resting in two golden spouts, explains that the oil ran thence into the bowl and through the forty-nine pipes to the lamps, rejects the received through on grammatical grounds, and identifies the two sons of oil as the priest and the prince whose joint labour secures the nation's prosperity; Keil and Delitzsch add nothing beyond the text of the exchange.

Gill declines to choose among the readings of the two anointed ones, canvassing the gifts and graces of the Spirit, Christ and the Spirit, and the open query whether it be Christ and the Comforter, or Christ in his two natures, or Christ in his two offices.

Clarke takes the two for the high priest and the governor, ministering in the ecclesiastical and the civil state, and is candid that the whole hieroglyphic may not be comprehensible; Wesley takes them for Christ and the Holy Spirit, both sent by the Father and standing ready to go.

Henry marks the difference between the two questions, tracks grace as communicated by word and ordinance rather than as resident in the tree, and notes that the angel made the prophet own his ignorance before informing him.

debates.question: Who are the two anointed ones, the sons of oil?

positions.position: The high priest and the governor, the one ministering in the ecclesiastical and the other in the civil state.
Christ and the Holy Spirit, both sent by the Father.
Undecided among several readings: the gifts and graces of the Spirit, Christ and the Spirit, Christ in his two natures, or Christ in his two offices.
Either, according to what the candlestick is taken to be: magistracy and ministry if the visible church, Christ and the Spirit if the church of the first-born.

debates.question: What are the two golden pipes and what passes through them?

positions.position: Better spouts than pipes: two golden spouts turned upward beside the bowl, in which the clusters rest and pour out the golden oil of themselves.
Pipes fastened to the bowl with a hole through its side, letting the oil distilled from the branches run in.

outliers.claim: Rejects the English rendering through as inadmissible because the definite article is prefixed to the participle, and records that the old Greek read the gold as golden funnels rather than golden oil, turning the participle active.
